    Chapter 14: Backtest Statistics¶

    AFML Ch. 14 -- Sharpe ratio adjustments and performance metrics.

    A raw Sharpe ratio can be misleading when returns are non-normal or when many strategies have been tested. This notebook covers the full toolkit for evaluating backtests: the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR) accounts for higher moments, the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) corrects for multiple testing, and drawdown analysis quantifies tail risk.

    This notebook demonstrates:

    • Sharpe ratio (annualized)
    • Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR)
    • Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR)
    • Drawdown analysis
    • HHI concentration
    • Hit ratio
    In [1]:
    Copied!

import pymlfinance
import pymlfinance.polars

    Generate Synthetic Strategy Returns¶

    We simulate 500 daily returns with a small positive drift and inject fat tails (20 random days with 3x returns) to make the distribution more realistic.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    n = 500
# Strategy with slight positive drift
returns = np.random.randn(n) * 0.01 + 0.0003
# Add some fat tails
returns[np.random.choice(n, 20, replace=False)] *= 3.0

print(f"Generated {n} daily returns")
print(f"  Mean: {np.mean(returns):.6f}, Std: {np.std(returns):.6f}")
    n = 500 # Strategy with slight positive drift returns = np.random.randn(n) * 0.01 + 0.0003 # Add some fat tails returns[np.random.choice(n, 20, replace=False)] *= 3.0 print(f"Generated {n} daily returns") print(f" Mean: {np.mean(returns):.6f}, Std: {np.std(returns):.6f}")
    Generated 500 daily returns
  Mean: 0.000353, Std: 0.011380

    Sharpe Ratio¶

    The annualized Sharpe ratio scales mean return by volatility and the square root of the number of periods per year.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    sr = pymlfinance.backtesting.sharpe_ratio(returns)
print(f"Annualized Sharpe ratio: {sr:.4f}")
    sr = pymlfinance.backtesting.sharpe_ratio(returns) print(f"Annualized Sharpe ratio: {sr:.4f}")

    Higher Moments & Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio¶

    Skewness and kurtosis affect the reliability of the Sharpe ratio estimate. PSR gives the probability that the true Sharpe ratio exceeds a benchmark, accounting for these higher moments.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    skew = pymlfinance.core.skewness(returns)
kurt = pymlfinance.core.kurtosis(returns)
print(f"Skewness: {skew:.4f}")
print(f"Excess Kurtosis: {kurt:.4f}")

# PSR uses the per-period (non-annualized) Sharpe ratio
sr_per_period = np.mean(returns) / np.std(returns, ddof=1)

psr = pymlfinance.backtesting.probabilistic_sharpe_ratio(
    observed_sr=sr_per_period,
    benchmark_sr=0.0,
    n_observations=n,
    skewness=skew,
    kurtosis=kurt
)
print(f"\nPer-period SR: {sr_per_period:.4f} (annualized: {sr:.4f})")
print(f"PSR(SR > 0): {psr:.4f}")
print(f"Interpretation: {psr:.0%} probability that true SR > 0")
    skew = pymlfinance.core.skewness(returns) kurt = pymlfinance.core.kurtosis(returns) print(f"Skewness: {skew:.4f}") print(f"Excess Kurtosis: {kurt:.4f}") # PSR uses the per-period (non-annualized) Sharpe ratio sr_per_period = np.mean(returns) / np.std(returns, ddof=1) psr = pymlfinance.backtesting.probabilistic_sharpe_ratio( observed_sr=sr_per_period, benchmark_sr=0.0, n_observations=n, skewness=skew, kurtosis=kurt ) print(f"\nPer-period SR: {sr_per_period:.4f} (annualized: {sr:.4f})") print(f"PSR(SR > 0): {psr:.4f}") print(f"Interpretation: {psr:.0%} probability that true SR > 0")
    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    # PSR with different per-period benchmarks
benchmarks = [0.0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05]
psr_values = []
for bench in benchmarks:
    p = pymlfinance.backtesting.probabilistic_sharpe_ratio(
        sr_per_period, bench, n, skew, kurt
    )
    psr_values.append(p)
    print(f"PSR(SR > {bench}): {p:.4f}")
    # PSR with different per-period benchmarks benchmarks = [0.0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05] psr_values = [] for bench in benchmarks: p = pymlfinance.backtesting.probabilistic_sharpe_ratio( sr_per_period, bench, n, skew, kurt ) psr_values.append(p) print(f"PSR(SR > {bench}): {p:.4f}")

    Visualisation: Sharpe Ratio Comparison¶

    A bar chart showing PSR at different benchmark levels. As the benchmark increases, the probability of exceeding it drops.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
colors = ["seagreen" if p > 0.5 else "tomato" for p in psr_values]
ax.bar([f"SR > {b}" for b in benchmarks], psr_values, color=colors, edgecolor="black")
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, label="50% threshold")
ax.set_ylabel("Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio")
ax.set_title(f"PSR at Different Benchmarks (per-period SR = {sr_per_period:.4f})")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis="y")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5)) colors = ["seagreen" if p > 0.5 else "tomato" for p in psr_values] ax.bar([f"SR > {b}" for b in benchmarks], psr_values, color=colors, edgecolor="black") ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, label="50% threshold") ax.set_ylabel("Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio") ax.set_title(f"PSR at Different Benchmarks (per-period SR = {sr_per_period:.4f})") ax.legend() ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis="y") ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05) plt.tight_layout() plt.show()

    Deflated Sharpe Ratio¶

    When multiple strategies have been tested, DSR adjusts for the selection bias. It penalises the Sharpe ratio based on the number of trials and the variance of Sharpe ratios across trials.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    n_trials = 20
trial_srs = [np.mean(r := np.random.randn(n) * 0.01 + 0.0002) / np.std(r, ddof=1)
             for _ in range(n_trials - 1)]
trial_srs.append(sr_per_period)  # include our strategy
sr_std = np.std(trial_srs)

dsr = pymlfinance.backtesting.deflated_sharpe_ratio(
    observed_sr=sr_per_period,
    sr_std=sr_std,
    n_observations=n,
    n_trials=n_trials,
    skewness=skew,
    kurtosis=kurt
)
print(f"After testing {n_trials} strategies:")
print(f"DSR = {dsr:.4f}")
print(f"(Accounts for multiple testing bias)")
    n_trials = 20 trial_srs = [np.mean(r := np.random.randn(n) * 0.01 + 0.0002) / np.std(r, ddof=1) for _ in range(n_trials - 1)] trial_srs.append(sr_per_period) # include our strategy sr_std = np.std(trial_srs) dsr = pymlfinance.backtesting.deflated_sharpe_ratio( observed_sr=sr_per_period, sr_std=sr_std, n_observations=n, n_trials=n_trials, skewness=skew, kurtosis=kurt ) print(f"After testing {n_trials} strategies:") print(f"DSR = {dsr:.4f}") print(f"(Accounts for multiple testing bias)")

    Drawdown Analysis¶

    Drawdowns measure the peak-to-trough decline in cumulative returns. Maximum drawdown and time under water are key risk metrics.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    dd = pymlfinance.backtesting.compute_drawdowns(returns)
print(f"Max drawdown: {dd.max_drawdown:.4f} ({dd.max_drawdown:.2%})")
print(f"Max drawdown duration: {dd.max_drawdown_duration} bars")
dd_series = np.array(dd.drawdown_series)
print(f"Average drawdown: {np.mean(dd_series):.4f}")
tuw = np.array(dd.time_under_water)
print(f"Avg time under water: {np.mean(tuw):.1f} bars")
    dd = pymlfinance.backtesting.compute_drawdowns(returns) print(f"Max drawdown: {dd.max_drawdown:.4f} ({dd.max_drawdown:.2%})") print(f"Max drawdown duration: {dd.max_drawdown_duration} bars") dd_series = np.array(dd.drawdown_series) print(f"Average drawdown: {np.mean(dd_series):.4f}") tuw = np.array(dd.time_under_water) print(f"Avg time under water: {np.mean(tuw):.1f} bars")
    Max drawdown: 0.1880 (18.80%)
Max drawdown duration: 201 bars
Average drawdown: 0.0749
Avg time under water: 60.6 bars

    Visualisation: Cumulative Returns with Drawdown Overlay¶

    The top panel shows cumulative returns; the bottom panel shows the drawdown series (always positive, measuring peak-to-trough decline).

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    cum_returns = np.cumprod(1 + returns) - 1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 8), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]})

# Cumulative returns
axes[0].plot(cum_returns, linewidth=1.5, color="steelblue")
axes[0].fill_between(range(len(cum_returns)), cum_returns, alpha=0.2, color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Cumulative Return")
axes[0].set_title("Cumulative Returns")
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Drawdown series
axes[1].fill_between(range(len(dd_series)), dd_series, color="tomato", alpha=0.7)
axes[1].plot(dd_series, linewidth=0.8, color="darkred")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Bar")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Drawdown")
axes[1].set_title(f"Drawdowns (max = {dd.max_drawdown:.2%})")
axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    cum_returns = np.cumprod(1 + returns) - 1 fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 8), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]}) # Cumulative returns axes[0].plot(cum_returns, linewidth=1.5, color="steelblue") axes[0].fill_between(range(len(cum_returns)), cum_returns, alpha=0.2, color="steelblue") axes[0].set_ylabel("Cumulative Return") axes[0].set_title("Cumulative Returns") axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3) # Drawdown series axes[1].fill_between(range(len(dd_series)), dd_series, color="tomato", alpha=0.7) axes[1].plot(dd_series, linewidth=0.8, color="darkred") axes[1].set_xlabel("Bar") axes[1].set_ylabel("Drawdown") axes[1].set_title(f"Drawdowns (max = {dd.max_drawdown:.2%})") axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.tight_layout() plt.show()

    Hit Ratio¶

    The hit ratio (win rate) is the fraction of returns that are positive. A high hit ratio does not guarantee profitability if losses are large.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    hr = pymlfinance.backtesting.hit_ratio(returns)
print(f"Win rate: {hr:.4f} ({hr:.1%})")
    hr = pymlfinance.backtesting.hit_ratio(returns) print(f"Win rate: {hr:.4f} ({hr:.1%})")
    Win rate: 0.5220 (52.2%)

    HHI Concentration¶

    The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index measures concentration. Applied to absolute returns, it shows whether P&L is driven by a few large bets (high HHI) or distributed evenly across time (low HHI).

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    hhi_val = pymlfinance.backtesting.hhi(np.abs(returns) / np.sum(np.abs(returns)))
pos_hhi, neg_hhi = pymlfinance.backtesting.hhi_concentration(returns)
print(f"HHI of |returns|: {hhi_val:.6f}")
print(f"Positive return HHI: {pos_hhi:.6f}")
print(f"Negative return HHI: {neg_hhi:.6f}")
print(f"(Lower HHI = more diversified across time)")
    hhi_val = pymlfinance.backtesting.hhi(np.abs(returns) / np.sum(np.abs(returns))) pos_hhi, neg_hhi = pymlfinance.backtesting.hhi_concentration(returns) print(f"HHI of |returns|: {hhi_val:.6f}") print(f"Positive return HHI: {pos_hhi:.6f}") print(f"Negative return HHI: {neg_hhi:.6f}") print(f"(Lower HHI = more diversified across time)")
    HHI of |returns|: 0.003605
Positive return HHI: 0.007146
Negative return HHI: 0.007260
(Lower HHI = more diversified across time)

    Polars API¶

    The same statistics are available as Polars expressions via the .ml namespace for efficient column-wise computation.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    df = pl.DataFrame({"returns": returns})
stats = df.select(
    pl.col("returns").ml.sharpe_ratio().alias("sharpe"),
    pl.col("returns").ml.hit_ratio().alias("hit_ratio"),
    pl.col("returns").ml.hhi().alias("hhi"),
)
print(stats)

dd_df = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("returns").ml.compute_drawdowns().alias("drawdown"),
)
print(f"Drawdown series (first 5): {dd_df['drawdown'].head(5).to_list()}")
    df = pl.DataFrame({"returns": returns}) stats = df.select( pl.col("returns").ml.sharpe_ratio().alias("sharpe"), pl.col("returns").ml.hit_ratio().alias("hit_ratio"), pl.col("returns").ml.hhi().alias("hhi"), ) print(stats) dd_df = df.with_columns( pl.col("returns").ml.compute_drawdowns().alias("drawdown"), ) print(f"Drawdown series (first 5): {dd_df['drawdown'].head(5).to_list()}")
